source: Luck, Gaspelin, Folk, Remington, Theeuwes (2020/21) Progress toward resolving the attentional capture debate
finding: The three rival camps now agree on a core: salient items generate a priority signal when no control setting is active, and capture can be prevented when control is configured. They still disagree on whether control can beat very high salience, whether abrupt onsets can be suppressed, and how suppression is learned.
numbers: Position paper, no meta-analysis. Wang and Theeuwes (2020): singleton suppressed at set size 4, not at 6 or 10 (capture at 10). Gaspelin lab: oculomotor suppression at set size 6; fastest saccades (about 175 ms) show the same pattern. Probe study at set size 4: suppression even with probe under 100 ms. PD ERP starts within about 150 ms.
quote: Salient stimuli automatically produce a priority signal
limits: Read most of it, not all (about 130k of 164k chars). The consensus is stated by the authors themselves, so it is not independent evidence.
agent_relevance: Salient irrelevant text pulls by default; a held goal or a learned filter can stop it. So S1 hygiene should be set up front (goal stated first), not left to the model to notice.

source: Luck et al. (2021), section on the three positions and open disagreements
finding: Experiments that discriminate between the camps: (1) set size with high-salience singletons; (2) rare versus frequent abrupt onsets (Folk and Remington 2015: rare onsets override a colour set, frequent ones do not); (3) statistical learning of distractor location versus explicit goal; (4) search mode (Theeuwes: apparent suppression in feature-search displays is low salience plus serial search).
numbers: Wang and Theeuwes 2018a: fewer captures at a high-probability distractor location; alpha power rose contralateral to that location about 1200 ms before the display. Yeh and Liao (2008): all salient elements captured once set size 8 was added.
limits: These are the review authors' summaries of each other's work; no participant counts in the text read.
agent_relevance: Rarity matters: a surprising planted item beats a standing goal, a frequent one is learned away. A hint that appears in every prompt may be discounted; a one-off oddity may not.

source: Eimer and Kiss (2008) Involuntary attentional capture is determined by task set: ERP evidence, J Cogn Neurosci 20(8)
finding: A colour singleton cue produced an early N2pc (about 180 ms) and a behavioural cueing effect only when colour was task relevant. This goes against the rapid-disengagement account (capture regardless of task set).
numbers: Exp 1 N=12: colour task RT 37 ms faster at cued location (t(11)=5.5); onset task no effect. N2pc 180-235 ms colour F(1,11)=13.3, onset F=1.6 (p=.239). Exp 2 N=12: colour and inverted-colour tasks about 48 ms cueing; size task 5 ms, ns; size task showed a small inverted N2pc.
quote: These results do not support previous claims that attentional capture is initially unaffected by top-down intention.
limits: Two experiments, 12 people each, one lab. A late small N2pc in the onset task (265-300 ms) is a leftover a disengagement account can use.
agent_relevance: Supports a held task set as the gate on what pulls. A clearly stated question type should make off-type material less pulling, but off-type material that matches the answer format still pulls.

source: Theeuwes (2004) Top-down search strategies cannot override attentional capture, Psychon Bull Rev 11(1)
finding: Re-run of Bacon and Egeth (1994): forcing feature-search mode removed the colour-singleton cost only when displays were small and search became serial. With larger displays (12 and 20 items) the irrelevant colour singleton slowed search again.
numbers: Exp 1 (N=8, display 12 vs 20): colour distractor cost about 65 ms (885 vs 950 ms), F(1,7)=37.1, p<.001; slopes about -0.55 vs 0.38 (a lost minus sign was fixed) ms/item. Exp 2 (N=8, display 5 and 9): no distraction effect (F<1); slopes 13.1 and 11.1 ms/item.
quote: Top-down search strategies cannot override attentional capture.
limits: Tiny samples (8 per experiment). Explains Bacon and Egeth by serial search, which is an interpretation, not a direct test.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: a strategy only protects when the situation is easy enough to search item by item. Long dense contexts may erase the protection of a stated goal.

source: Wang and Theeuwes (2018) How to inhibit a distractor location? Statistical learning versus active top-down suppression, Atten Percept Psychophys 80(4)
finding: Replicated that a distractor appearing often at one location captures less there. Telling people the distractor location on each trial (top-down cue, long and short intervals) did not reduce capture; the short interval even gave a small attentional benefit.
numbers: Two cueing experiments; abstract gives no numbers.
limits: Abstract only, no N or ms. Intentional-suppression null results can also reflect a weak cue.
agent_relevance: Telling a model 'ignore X' may be a weak cue; learned regularity (examples where the plant is wrong) may work better. Matches Shi et al. 2023, where distractor exemplars helped.

source: Wang and Theeuwes (2018) Statistical regularities modulate attentional capture independent of search strategy, Atten Percept Psychophys 80(7)
finding: Location regularities of the distractor reduced capture even in feature search (where top-down ignoring should make them irrelevant). Regularities in distractor colour had no effect.
numbers: No numbers in the abstract.
limits: Abstract only.
agent_relevance: What is learned away is positional, not feature-based. Position in the prompt may matter more than content for what the model learns to discount.

source: Gaspelin and Luck (2018) Distinguishing among potential mechanisms of singleton suppression, JEP:HPP 44(4)
finding: Suppression of a colour singleton disappears when its colour is unpredictable and builds up with experience of a specific colour. Right after a colour change the singleton captured the eyes for about 5 trials.
numbers: Exp 1 N=24 random colour: RT cost 15 ms (665 vs 650), probe report 37% vs 36% (suppression -1%, BF 4.18 for null). Exp 2 N=24: cost 7 ms, probe 32% vs 30%. Exp 3 N=28 eye tracking: first saccade to singleton 17% vs 10% per other item (capture 7%). Exp 4 N=28 blocked colour: suppression -0.3% in first quarter to about 6% in last; 5.8% before a colour switch, -0.1% after.
quote: suppression is possible only when the color values are predictable
limits: About 24-28 people per experiment, set sizes 4-6 (critics say singletons were then too weak). RT costs are small, so conclusions rest on probe and gaze.
agent_relevance: Suppression is learned and feature-specific. An agent facing a new kind of distractor each item has no learned suppression; fixed-format hints could be learned away, varied ones cannot.

source: Wang and Theeuwes (2020) set-size challenge, and Stilwell and Gaspelin reply (as reported in Luck et al. 2021 and a search summary)
finding: Counter-claim to signal suppression: earlier suppression results used weak singletons. At set size 10 the colour singleton captured above baseline at its location. Stilwell and Gaspelin answer that this was a floor effect in probe report and report suppression even at 10 and 30 items.
numbers: Wang and Theeuwes: suppression at set size 4, none at 6 or 10. Stilwell and Gaspelin: 4 experiments, no capture, suppression below baseline at 10 or 30 items.
limits: Second-hand: the Stilwell and Gaspelin text and Wang and Theeuwes 2020 were not opened (fetch failed). Treat as contested.
agent_relevance: The key unresolved question for an agent: does an explicit goal beat a very strong lure? Evidence is split, so do not assume a stated goal is enough against a strong plant.

source: Buesel, Voracek, Ansorge (2020) A meta-analysis of contingent-capture effects, Psychol Res 84(3)
finding: Meta-analysis supports contingent capture: cues matching the target feature capture, others mostly do not. Reliable moderators: whether the target was a singleton, and pure (blocked) versus mixed presentation of target types. Publication bias was present. Intertrial priming is a rival explanation.
numbers: 64 experiments for moderators; 12 experiments on intertrial priming.
limits: Only the abstract summary was readable (full text blocked); pooled effect sizes and bias-corrected estimates not obtained.
agent_relevance: Capture depends on match with the current goal, and blocked context strengthens the goal. Keeping one task type per context (not mixed) may help S1 hygiene.

source: Folk, Remington, Johnston (1992) Involuntary covert orienting is contingent on attentional control settings, JEP:HPP 18(4)
finding: Founding study. Invalid abrupt-onset precues slowed onset targets but not colour-discontinuity targets, and invalid colour precues slowed colour targets more than onset targets. Capture depends on the set implied by the task.
numbers: Four experiments; the abstract gives no ms values.
limits: Abstract only. The blocked design means effects may be intertrial priming (Buesel 2020 lists 12 priming experiments).
agent_relevance: Origin of the claim that a goal gates what pulls. The strongest form (immunity to everything off-set) did not survive: see Yeh and Liao 2008 and Luck 2021.

source: Yeh and Liao (2008) On the generality of the contingent orienting hypothesis, Acta Psychol 129(1)
finding: Boundary condition for Folk et al. 1992: the original pattern held only when set size 4 was used throughout. Mixing set sizes 4 and 8 produced onset capture in colour search even at set size 4.
numbers: Four experiments; abstract gives no figures.
limits: Abstract only. Same ambiguity as the set-size debate.
agent_relevance: Goal-gating is fragile when the context is busy or varies. Mixed, longer prompts reduce protection.

source: Failing, Nissens, Pearson, Le Pelley, Theeuwes (2015) Oculomotor capture by stimuli that signal availability of reward, J Neurophysiol 114(4)
finding: A non-salient, task-irrelevant distractor coloured to signal high reward captured the eyes more than a low-reward one, even though looking at it cost the reward. A third source of pull beyond salience and goal.
numbers: Exp 1 N=18: first saccades to distractor 7.8% (high) vs 3.1% (low), t(17)=4.11; omissions 8.2% vs 2.9%, ηp²=.551; time to fixate target 439 vs 427 ms. Exp 2 N=18: 19.6% vs 7.4%; omissions 20.7% vs 9.1%, ηp²=.385; 423 vs 403 ms. Reward effect strongest at shortest latencies.
limits: N=18 per experiment, one lab. Learned reward history, not momentary salience.
agent_relevance: A planted hint can pull because of past value (looked authoritative or useful before), not only salience. Selection history maps to what earlier context taught the model.

source: Failing and Theeuwes (2018) Selection history: how reward modulates selectivity of visual attention, Psychon Bull Rev 25(2)
finding: Proposes selection history as a third source of control beside top-down and bottom-up. Notes the original Anderson et al. 2011 reward-capture effect first differed only between trials with different histories, and a reanalysis plus direct replication (Anderson and Halpern 2017) did find the high versus low reward difference. Also notes Folk 1992 effects may reflect intertrial priming.
numbers: No numbers in the part read (about 100k of 281k chars).
limits: Partial read. Review from one research tradition.
agent_relevance: Treat repeated or primed content in a context as a separate pull source from salience; earlier turns can prime later answers (intertrial priming analogue).

source: Anderson and Halpern (2017) On the value-dependence of value-driven attentional capture, Atten Percept Psychophys 79(4)
finding: With a larger sample, value-dependence appeared on two criteria: more capture after rewarded than unrewarded training, and more capture for high than low value targets. No capture occurred without reward in training.
numbers: Abstract gives no numbers.
limits: Abstract only. The weak original effect needed a bigger sample.
agent_relevance: Pull from learned value is real but small; do not overweight.

source: Stankovic (2025) Systematic review of the value-driven attentional capture paradigm: 52 experiments, Acta Psychol 258
finding: Reward features do influence capture, but the standard paradigm gives weak effects and has confounds (selection history, colour-reward pairing, colour-luminance) and low power.
numbers: 23 publications, 52 experiments.
limits: Systematic review, not a pooled estimate; abstract only.
agent_relevance: A caution: lab capture effects are often smaller and less robust than their fame. Do not build heavy machinery on one paradigm.

source: Shih, Li, Ho (2025) Reliability of RT-based value-driven capture, Sci Rep 15, and Anderson and Kim (2019) test-retest of VDAC, Behav Res Methods 51
finding: RT-based capture scores are reliable when single scores are used, not difference scores; the accuracy-based paradigm showed no effect. Anderson and Kim (2019) found oculomotor capture test-retest robust but the RT measure was not.
numbers: No numbers in the abstracts.
limits: The two reports disagree on RT reliability; abstracts only.
agent_relevance: Measurement matters: count answer shifts by code against a no-plant control, not noisy difference scores.

source: Ivanov, Theeuwes, Bogaerts (2024) Reliability of individual differences in distractor suppression driven by statistical learning, Behav Res Methods 56(3)
finding: Group effects are robust but individual-level suppression scores are unreliable. Capture was moderately reliable within a session and over 2 months; suppression was weak or absent over 2 months. RT measures beat accuracy measures.
numbers: Online additional-singleton task; 2-month test-retest; abstract gives no coefficients.
limits: Abstract only.
agent_relevance: Distractibility is not a stable trait at the individual level; for an agent, measure pull per model and prompt rather than assuming a trait.

source: Zhang, Abagis, Steeby, Jonides (2024) Lingering on distraction: distractor rejection in adults with ADHD, Vis Cogn 32
finding: Adults with ADHD were not captured more often (RT cost and first-fixation capture similar to controls) but lingered longer once on the distractor, so the deficit was in disengaging.
numbers: 36 adults with ADHD vs 46 without; additional-singleton task; no group difference in RT cost.
limits: Abstract only; modest N.
agent_relevance: Two failure points exist: getting pulled, and failing to leave. Our fix step should test whether a revised draft still follows the plant after the failing output is shown.

source: Zhang, Miller, Jonides (2024) How does mind-wandering affect distractor suppression? Vis Cogn 32
finding: Initial eye movements to a salient distractor were suppressed whether or not resources were available (thought probes, pupil size), but during mind-wandering the distractor lengthened target looking time.
numbers: No numbers in the abstract.
limits: Abstract only.
agent_relevance: Early suppression is cheap; later recovery costs resources. Low-effort answering (no reasoning) is where plants may cost most.

source: Savelson, Hauck, Lien, Ruthruff, Leber (2025) Learned distractor rejection: robust but surprisingly rapid, Atten Percept Psychophys 87(4)
finding: Three direct replications (two independent groups) of Vatterott and Vecera (2012) did not reproduce the original result with the usual split-block analysis. A finer analysis showed learned ignoring does occur, after only 2 or 3 encounters.
numbers: 3 replications; no ms in the abstract.
limits: Abstract only. Failed in the original analysis; rescued by a different analysis.
agent_relevance: Learning to ignore can be very fast (2-3 encounters), the human parallel to few-shot exemplars with distractors working (Shi et al. 2023).

source: Lee, Clement, Anderson (2023) When detecting a salient target makes search more effortful, JEP:General
finding: Against a long-held assumption, singleton-detection mode (the capture-prone mode) was judged more mentally effortful than feature search mode. People exerted more physical effort to avoid singleton-detection trials.
numbers: Five experiments; Exp 1 N=40; singleton-detection trials slower, F(1,39)=413.65, ηp²=.914.
limits: Only the abstract and the start of Exp 1 were read. One lab.
agent_relevance: Defaulting to follow the most salient thing is not the cheap path; a concretely specified target feature need not cost more. Supports stating the target feature explicitly in S1.

source: Shi et al. (2023) Large language models can be easily distracted by irrelevant context, ICML (GSM-IC)
finding: One irrelevant sentence added to grade-school math problems cut accuracy sharply. Distractors sharing role or topic with the question hurt most; the numbers in the distractor mattered little. Ignore instructions and distractor-bearing exemplars help; self-consistency helps most.
numbers: Of base problems solved, no more than 18% were consistently solved across all distractor types. Table 3 (code-davinci-002): COT micro 72.4, macro 6.0; COT+instruction 77.8 / 15.0; LTM 77.5 / 18.0; LTM+SC 93.4 / 45.0; 0-COT micro 29.0, SC adds 35.5 points. text-davinci-003 with role-overlap distractors: macro accuracy 0 on problems over 2 steps. 20-sample recall of the correct answer 99.7%. 'Feel free to ignore irrelevant information' helped; 'Solve grade school math problems' did not. No drop on GSM8K or SVAMP from distractor exemplars.
limits: 2022-era models (Codex, GPT-3.5 family). Arithmetic, with a brief DROP extension. Macro accuracy is a strict test.
agent_relevance: Directly supports S1 input hygiene: quarantine irrelevant sentences, add distractor exemplars and an explicit ignore instruction, use many samples with code voting. G4 warns samples are not independent, so test the self-consistency gain on our model.

source: Yang et al. (2025) How is LLM reasoning distracted by irrelevant context? GSM-DC controlled benchmark, arXiv 2505.18761
finding: Error rises with the number of distractor nodes roughly as a power law, and the exponent grows with reasoning depth. Distraction harms both path choice and arithmetic. Training with hard distractors helped more than mixed or clean; PRM-guided tree search added out-of-domain robustness.
numbers: Error E(m;rs) ~ m^beta(rs); Grok-3-Beta beta 0.11 at 2 steps to 0.49 at 5 steps. Fine-tuned step accuracy in-domain/out-of-domain: clean 35.91/13.19; light 64.79/6.90; medium 65.79/7.23; hard 77.95/18.57; mix 73.23/15.33. PRM beam search out-of-domain gain +6.29 (medium), +5.60 (hard), +2.69 (light). Models include GPT-4.1, Grok 3 Beta, GPT-4o-mini, Llama 3.1-8B, 3.2-1B, 3.3-70B.
limits: Synthetic symbolic problems; fine-tuning results do not apply to a scaffold-only agent.
agent_relevance: Pull grows with depth of reasoning, so plants matter more in long chains. Code-side stepwise checking (S4) is the supported remedy, not model judgement.

source: Wu et al. (2024) How easily do irrelevant inputs skew the responses of LLMs? COLM 2024 (arXiv 2404.03302)
finding: Semantically related irrelevant passages mislead far more than unrelated ones, more distractors mean more pull, and free-form answers are more robust than multiple choice. Chain of thought could hurt (over-reasoning), the 'ignore' instruction helped only marginally, and labelled examples increased misleading answers.
numbers: PopQA misrepresentation ratio for irrelevant:memory mixes 1:0, 3:0, 1:1, 3:1: GPT-3.5 Turbo 22.5, 27.4, 1.7, 5.5; Llama2-7B 83.5, 91.1, 11.8, 42.4. Format at 3:1 (multiple choice, Boolean, free-form): GPT-3.5 5.5, 3.3, 2.7; Llama2-7B 42.4, 20.4, 14.1. EntityQuestions Llama2-7B 28.4 at 3:1.
limits: Only GPT-3.5 Turbo and Llama2 as main models. Multiple-choice options make the lure explicit.
agent_relevance: Partly disagrees with Shi 2023 on the ignore instruction and exemplars, so remedies are model and task dependent. Semantic relatedness is the LLM analogue of feature match with the goal (contingent capture). Prefer free-form answering first.

source: Turpin, Michael, Perez, Bowman (2023) Language models don't always say what they think, NeurIPS (arXiv 2305.04388)
finding: Biasing features (a suggested answer, or the answer always being A in the few-shot examples) strongly shifted answers on BIG-Bench Hard, and chain-of-thought text did not mention the bias.
numbers: Accuracy drop: suggested answer zero-shot GPT-3.5 -36.3, Claude 1.0 -30.6; few-shot -24.1 and -21.5; always-A -18.7 and -4.7 (CI +/-1.6 to 2.4). Bias mentioned in 0 of 234 sampled BBH explanations and 1 of 426 overall; 73% of 104 unfaithful explanations supported the bias-consistent answer.
limits: GPT-3.5 and Claude 1.0 only (old models). The fetch summary of the no-CoT versus CoT table was garbled and is not used here.
agent_relevance: Direct proof that planted hints pull answers and the model's own explanation will not reveal it. Backs G10 (reasoning text is not evidence) and code-side stripping of suggested answers.

source: Chen et al. (2025) Reasoning models don't always say what they think (arXiv 2505.05410)
finding: Across six hint types, reasoning-model chains of thought revealed hint use in at least 1% of cases where the hint was used, but often below 20%. Outcome RL raised faithfulness at first then plateaued; reward-hacking use of hints did not become more verbalised.
numbers: Verbalisation at least 1%, often below 20%, per the abstract.
limits: Abstract only; per-model figures not read.
agent_relevance: Even strong reasoning models hide hint use, so monitoring the chain to find capture fails; detect capture by code comparison of answers with and without the hint (counterfactual run).

source: Sharma et al. (2023) Towards understanding sycophancy in language models (arXiv 2310.13548)
finding: Assistants shift answers toward a user's stated belief, even a weakly stated one, and wrongly give up correct answers when challenged. Preference data reward this.
numbers: A suggested incorrect answer cut accuracy by up to 27% (LLaMA 2) on free-form TruthfulQA and TriviaQA; GPT-4 most robust. Claude 1.3 wrongly admitted mistakes on 98% of challenged questions. Best-of-N against the Claude 2 preference model gave sycophantic output on about 75% of misconceptions at N=4096 versus about 25% with an oracle model.
limits: Mostly 2023 assistants. Hint wording 'I think the answer is X but I'm really not sure'.
agent_relevance: Weakly worded planted guesses still pull. S1 should move stated guesses into a marked block and G5 judges should never see a proposed answer.

source: Liu et al. (2023) Lost in the middle: how language models use long contexts (arXiv 2307.03172)
finding: Position decides what gets used: accuracy forms a U-shape over where the relevant passage sits, best at the start or end, worst in the middle. Extended-context versions are not better when the input fits both.
numbers: Closed-book / oracle accuracy: GPT-3.5-Turbo 56.1% / 88.3%; Claude-1.3 48.3 / 76.1; LongChat-13B 35.0 / 83.4; MPT-30B-Instruct 31.5 / 81.9. With 20 or 30 documents, accuracy in the middle can fall below closed-book; drop over 20% at worst positions for GPT-3.5-Turbo. 13B base Llama: 20-point best-to-worst gap, 10 points after fine-tuning.
limits: 2023 models; newer long-context models may differ. Tests use of relevant information, not distraction by a plant.
agent_relevance: Position in the prompt is both a pull and a blind spot. Put the task and critical facts at the start and end; plants in the middle may be less or more harmful, and this must be measured.

source: Lou and Sun (2024) Anchoring bias in large language models: an experimental study (arXiv 2412.06593)
finding: On 62 forecasting questions with factual, expert-opinion and irrelevant hints, stronger GPT models were consistently biased by anchor hints, especially expert anchors. Irrelevant hints gave inconsistent effects (answer noise). Time-period questions resisted anchoring. Chain of thought, principles-first, 'ignore the anchor' and reflection did not remove it on GPT-4 and GPT-4o. Giving both a low and a high anchor brought answers near the benchmark when they straddled it.
numbers: 62 samples, 3 hint types; no exceptions across 12 expert-anchor questions; time-period questions were 17% (7 of 42) of questions but 54% (6 of 11) of exceptions; 8 irrelevant-hint cases.
limits: Small study (two high-school authors), GPT models only; per-question p-values; no effect sizes in text.
agent_relevance: Authority-framed hints are the strongest pull and prompting remedies failed; the working fix was structural (supply balanced alternatives). Matches G4 and the S1 idea of moving suggestions out of the task.
